summary.text: A 34-year-old Malaysian woman presented with abdominal pain after a recent cholecystectomy for necrotizing cholecystitis. A small pericardial effusion was found incidentally, and echocardiography showed severe global hypokinesis with a significantly reduced ejection fraction. After a week of antibiotics for presumed cholangitis she developed chest pain.

Work-up included CT pulmonary angiography, a normal coronary angiogram and cardiac MRI showing extensive subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement with a small left ventricular apical thrombus, treated with a heparin drip. Serology showed a positive lupus anticoagulant, elevated anticardiolipin and anti-beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies, normal complement and positive ANA.

Weeks later she returned with worsening dyspnea at rest, new proteinuria, oliguria and increased creatinine despite antibiotics, heart failure therapy and immunosuppression. Right ventricular biopsy was nondiagnostic, renal biopsy was consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy, ADAMTS13 activity was normal, and eculizumab 900 mg IV weekly was started with meningococcal prophylaxis.

Two months later she returned with severe sepsis, an acute mental status change with bilateral acute brain infarcts, status epilepticus, PEA arrests and a left wrist lesion whose biopsy suggested thrombotic microangiopathy. She received IVIG and rituximab with continued eculizumab, with temporary improvement in her cardiomyopathy allowing inotropes to be discontinued; her subsequent course was complicated by pneumonia, acute pancreatitis and hypotension during hemodialysis requiring vasopressor support.

Brain natriuretic peptide exceeded 5000 pg/mL, troponin-T reached 0.178 ng/mL, right heart catheterization values were consistent with cardiogenic shock and the last echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction below 20%. Given her condition, her family chose to transition to palliative care and she died.

summary.text: A 57-year-old Thai man with prior SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome complicated by stroke, pulmonary embolism, liver infarct, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, ITP, lupus cerebritis and chronic kidney disease presented with right upper quadrant and right flank pain for 6 days and acute encephalopathy. Concern arose for splanchnic thrombosis and ischemia.

Head CT was negative for hemorrhage or large infarct, ANA titer was 1:80 with negative dsDNA and ANCA and normal complement, and CT angiography showed new bilateral pulmonary emboli with liver and splenic infarcts but no renal involvement. High suspicion of CAPS-associated thrombotic microangiopathy remained given acute anuric renal failure.

He was started on continuous renal replacement therapy and received IVIG, pulse steroids, a heparin drip and eculizumab. About 10 days after hospitalization hemoglobin dropped with hypotension; CT showed retroperitoneal hematomas treated with gel foam embolization of the right lumbar arteries. Kidney function improved with diuresis. Bacteremia, Clostridium difficile infection and a urinary tract infection complicated the course, and anticoagulation changed from heparin to dalteparin before he went home with plans for bimonthly eculizumab.

Several months after discharge he developed worsening orthopnea. Echocardiography showed a severely reduced ejection fraction of 26% from a baseline of 50-55%, and cardiac MRI showed severe global hypokinesis without late gadolinium enhancement. Catheterization showed elevated filling pressures and reduced cardiac index; coronary angiography showed only mild single vessel disease, and troponin-T and pro-BNP were elevated. He was discharged on heart failure therapy and continued eculizumab, steroids and dalteparin.
